title: What Is the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and What Does It Do?

CRS Report R46240 — Introduction to the Federal Budget Process

claims.claim: The page explains what the CBO is and what it does
claims.sourceSpan: There is established an office of the Congress to be known as the Congressional Budget Office

claims.claim: The Congressional Budget Act prescribes the contents of a cost estimate
claims.sourceSpan: The Director of the Congressional Budget Office shall, to the extent practicable, prepare for each bill or resolution of a public character reported by any committee of the House of Representatives or the Senate (except the Committee on Appropriations of each House), and submit to such committee

claims.claim: It prescribes the horizon of the estimate
claims.sourceSpan: an estimate of the costs which would be incurred in carrying out such bill or resolution in the fiscal year in which it is to become effective and in each of the 4 fiscal years following such fiscal year, together with the basis for each such estimate

claims.claim: Estimates are measured against a baseline
claims.sourceSpan: The term "baseline" means the projection (described in section 907 of this title) of current-year levels of new budget authority, outlays, receipts, and the surplus or deficit into the budget year and the outyears.

claims.claim: CBO is required to price certain private-sector mandate costs
claims.sourceSpan: If the Director estimates that the direct cost of all Federal private sector mandates in the bill or joint resolution will equal or exceed $100,000,000 (adjusted annually for inflation) in the fiscal year in which any Federal private sector mandate in the bill or joint resolution (or in any necessary implementing regulation) would first be effective or in any of the 4 fiscal years following such fiscal year, the Director shall so state, specify the estimate, and briefly explain the basis of the estimate.

claims.claim: The CBO is established by statute as an office of the Congress
claims.sourceSpan: There is established an office of the Congress to be known as the Congressional Budget Office

claims.claim: That provision is section 201 of the Congressional Budget Act, enacted July 12, 1974
claims.sourceSpan: Pub. L. 93–344, title II, §201, July 12, 1974

claims.claim: The Director is appointed by the Speaker and the President pro tempore without regard to political affiliation
claims.sourceSpan: The Director shall be appointed by the Speaker of the House of Representatives and the President pro tempore of the Senate after considering recommendations received from the Committees on the Budget of the House and the Senate, without regard to political affiliation and solely on the basis of his fitness to perform his duties.

claims.claim: The Director's term is four years
claims.sourceSpan: The term of office of the Director shall be 4 years

claims.claim: Either House may remove the Director by resolution
claims.sourceSpan: The Director may be removed by either House by resolution.

claims.claim: Staff are also appointed without regard to political affiliation
claims.sourceSpan: All personnel of the Office shall be appointed without regard to political affiliation and solely on the basis of their fitness to perform their duties.

claims.claim: The primary duty is to give the Budget Committees information for matters in their jurisdiction
claims.sourceSpan: It shall be the primary duty and function of the Office to provide to the Committees on the Budget of both Houses information which will assist such committees in the discharge of all matters within their jurisdictions

claims.claim: That information covers the budget, appropriations bills and other bills providing budget authority or tax expenditures
claims.sourceSpan: information with respect to the budget, appropriation bills, and other bills authorizing or providing new budget authority or tax expenditures

claims.claim: Appropriations, Ways and Means and Finance may request assistance
claims.sourceSpan: At the request of the Committee on Appropriations of either House, the Committee on Ways and Means of the House of Representatives, or the Committee on Finance of the Senate, the Office shall provide to such Committee any information which will assist it in the discharge of matters within its jurisdiction

claims.claim: Individual Members may also request information
claims.sourceSpan: At the request of any Member of the House or Senate, the Office shall provide to such Member any information compiled in carrying out clauses (1) and (2) of subsection (a)

claims.field: What a Cost Estimate Must Contain
claims.claim: Section 653 is headed Analysis by Congressional Budget Office
claims.sourceSpan: Analysis by Congressional Budget Office

claims.field: What a Cost Estimate Must Contain
claims.claim: The Director must prepare an estimate for each reported public bill except those from Appropriations
claims.sourceSpan: The Director of the Congressional Budget Office shall, to the extent practicable, prepare for each bill or resolution of a public character reported by any committee of the House of Representatives or the Senate (except the Committee on Appropriations of each House), and submit to such committee

claims.field: What a Cost Estimate Must Contain
claims.claim: Item one: costs in the fiscal year of effect and each of the 4 following fiscal years, with the basis for each estimate
claims.sourceSpan: an estimate of the costs which would be incurred in carrying out such bill or resolution in the fiscal year in which it is to become effective and in each of the 4 fiscal years following such fiscal year, together with the basis for each such estimate

claims.field: What a Cost Estimate Must Contain
claims.claim: Item two: a comparison with any available committee or agency cost estimates
claims.sourceSpan: a comparison of the estimates of costs described in paragraph (1) with any available estimates of costs made by such committee or by any Federal agency

claims.field: What a Cost Estimate Must Contain
claims.claim: Item three: a description of each method for establishing a federal financial commitment
claims.sourceSpan: a description of each method for establishing a Federal financial commitment contained in such bill or resolution

claims.field: What a Cost Estimate Must Contain
claims.claim: The estimate is included in the committee report if timely submitted
claims.sourceSpan: The estimates, comparison, and description so submitted shall be included in the report accompanying such bill or resolution if timely submitted to such committee before such report is filed.

claims.field: What a Cost Estimate Must Contain
claims.claim: Budget resolutions have in recent practice often covered a 10-year period
claims.sourceSpan: In recent practice, budget resolutions have often covered a 10-year period.

claims.field: What a Cost Estimate Must Contain
claims.claim: Statutory PAYGO uses a five-year and a 10-year scorecard
claims.sourceSpan: To enforce Statutory PAYGO, OMB is required to record the budgetary effects of newly enacted revenue and direct spending legislation on two separate scorecards: one that covers a five-year period and one that covers a 10-year period.

claims.claim: The statutory definition of baseline is the projection of current-year levels into the budget year and outyears
claims.sourceSpan: The term "baseline" means the projection (described in section 907 of this title) of current-year levels of new budget authority, outlays, receipts, and the surplus or deficit into the budget year and the outyears.

claims.claim: CRS describes a baseline as an estimate of federal spending and receipts under existing law
claims.sourceSpan: A baseline is an estimate of federal spending and receipts during a fiscal year under existing law.

claims.claim: Cost estimates measure a proposal against baseline levels assumed under current law
claims.sourceSpan: When conducting cost estimates, CBO and JCT measure the budgetary effect of a legislative proposal in relation to projections of revenue and spending levels that are assumed to occur under current law, typically referred to as baseline levels.

claims.claim: Programs with current-year outlays above $50 million are assumed to continue past their expiration
claims.sourceSpan: any program with estimated current year outlays greater than $50 million is assumed to continue to operate under the terms of the law at the time of its expiration

claims.claim: Scorekeeping measures the budgetary effects of legislation against the baseline
claims.sourceSpan: Scorekeeping is the process of measuring the budgetary effects of pending and enacted legislation against the baseline.

claims.claim: Scorekeeping is the Budget Committees' responsibility with CBO's assistance
claims.sourceSpan: In the congressional budget process, scorekeeping is the responsibility of the House and Senate Budget Committees, acting with the assistance of CBO.

claims.claim: Discretionary appropriations means budgetary resources provided in appropriation Acts, except to fund direct-spending programs
claims.sourceSpan: The term "discretionary appropriations" means budgetary resources (except to fund direct-spending programs) provided in appropriation Acts.

claims.claim: Direct spending means budget authority provided other than by appropriation Acts, entitlement authority, and SNAP
claims.sourceSpan: The term "direct spending" means— (A) budget authority provided by law other than appropriation Acts; (B) entitlement authority; and (C) the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.

claims.claim: For revenue measures CBO must rely on Joint Committee on Taxation estimates
claims.sourceSpan: For revenue measures, CBO is required to rely on estimates provided by the Joint Committee on Taxation (Section 201(f) of the Budget Act).

claims.claim: The Byrd rule establishes six tests for extraneous matter
claims.sourceSpan: The Byrd rule establishes six tests used to identify extraneous matter.

claims.claim: A provision with no change in outlays or revenues is extraneous
claims.sourceSpan: It does not produce a change in outlays or revenues, including changes resulting from a change in the "terms and conditions" under which outlays are made or revenues are collected

claims.claim: A provision whose budgetary change is merely incidental is extraneous
claims.sourceSpan: It produces a change in outlays or revenues that is merely incidental to the non-budgetary components of the provision.

claims.claim: Reported measures must carry estimates of budgetary impact, calculated by CBO
claims.sourceSpan: Section 308(a) of the Budget Act requires that any measure reported by a committee include estimates of the budgetary impact of the proposed legislation. These estimates, usually in the form of a statement in the accompanying committee report or published separately in the Congressional Record , are calculated by CBO.

claims.claim: The Budget Committees must publish monthly summary scorekeeping reports
claims.sourceSpan: Section 308(b) of the 1974 Congressional Budget Act requires the Budget Committees to make available, to their respective chambers, monthly summary scorekeeping reports on the current status of congressional budget actions.

claims.claim: Conventional estimates include individual behavioural responses but not the macroeconomic effects that alter GDP
claims.sourceSpan: Generally, CBO and JCT estimates include projections of the budgetary effects that would result from proposed policy changes, and incorporate anticipated individual behavioral responses to the policy. The estimates do not typically include the macroeconomic effects of those individual behavioral responses that would alter gross domestic product (GDP).

claims.claim: Estimates that do include macroeconomic effects are called dynamic estimates or dynamic scores
claims.sourceSpan: These estimates are often referred to as dynamic estimates or dynamic scores .

claims.claim: Proponents argue dynamic estimates are more accurate and improve comparison of proposals
claims.sourceSpan: Proponents of dynamic estimates have argued that such estimates provide a more accurate assessment of budgetary impact than conventional scoring, and that they can improve Congress’s ability to compare competing policy proposals.

claims.claim: Opponents argue macroeconomic feedback estimates are too uncertain to rely on
claims.sourceSpan: Opponents of dynamic estimates argue that estimates of macroeconomic feedback effects are too uncertain to be relied upon as accurate projections of budgetary outcomes.

claims.claim: Published dynamic estimates have varied widely by model and assumptions
claims.sourceSpan: In some cases, published estimates showed wide variation in estimated results depending on the model type and assumptions.

claims.claim: Dynamic estimates were used only for informational purposes, not for compliance with budgetary rules
claims.sourceSpan: During this period, dynamic estimates were used only for informational purposes, as opposed to being used to determine whether Congress was complying with its budgetary rules.

claims.field: CBO and the Cost of Regulation
claims.claim: A Federal private sector mandate is any provision imposing an enforceable duty on the private sector, subject to two exceptions, or reducing an authorization of appropriations for compliance assistance
claims.sourceSpan: The term "Federal private sector mandate" means any provision in legislation, statute, or regulation that— (A) would impose an enforceable duty upon the private sector except— (i) a condition of Federal assistance; or (ii) a duty arising from participation in a voluntary Federal program; or (B) would reduce or eliminate the amount of authorization of appropriations for Federal financial assistance that will be provided to the private sector for the purposes of ensuring compliance with such duty.

claims.field: CBO and the Cost of Regulation
claims.claim: Its direct cost means the aggregate estimated amounts the private sector must spend to comply
claims.sourceSpan: in the case of a Federal private sector mandate, means the aggregate estimated amounts that the private sector will be required to spend in order to comply with the Federal private sector mandate

claims.field: CBO and the Cost of Regulation
claims.claim: CBO must state and explain private-sector mandate costs at or above $100,000,000, adjusted annually for inflation, including costs from any necessary implementing regulation
claims.sourceSpan: If the Director estimates that the direct cost of all Federal private sector mandates in the bill or joint resolution will equal or exceed $100,000,000 (adjusted annually for inflation) in the fiscal year in which any Federal private sector mandate in the bill or joint resolution (or in any necessary implementing regulation) would first be effective or in any of the 4 fiscal years following such fiscal year, the Director shall so state, specify the estimate, and briefly explain the basis of the estimate.

claims.field: CBO and the Cost of Regulation
claims.claim: The intergovernmental-mandate threshold is $50,000,000, adjusted annually for inflation
claims.sourceSpan: If the Director estimates that the direct cost of all Federal intergovernmental mandates in the bill or joint resolution will equal or exceed $50,000,000 (adjusted annually for inflation)

claims.field: CBO and the Cost of Regulation
claims.claim: Where a bill authorises appropriations for an intergovernmental mandate, the estimate runs up to 10 years beyond the effective date
claims.sourceSpan: the amount of new budget authority for each fiscal year for a period not to exceed 10 years beyond the effective date necessary for the direct cost of the intergovernmental mandate

claims.field: CBO and the Cost of Regulation
claims.claim: Where a reasonable estimate is not feasible the Director must say so and give reasons
claims.sourceSpan: shall not make the estimate, but shall report in the statement that the reasonable estimate cannot be made

claims.claim: The statute guarantees the five-year figures with their basis, the comparison, and the description of each method
claims.sourceSpan: The estimates, comparison, and description so submitted shall be included in the report accompanying such bill or resolution if timely submitted to such committee before such report is filed.

claims.claim: Congressional rules requiring dynamic estimates have existed in most years since 1997 — the period CRS then describes as informational-only
claims.sourceSpan: In most years since 1997, congressional rules have existed that require JCT or CBO to provide dynamic estimates under certain circumstances.

claims.claim: It is delay on the regular appropriations acts that opens the funding gap behind a shutdown
claims.sourceSpan: When action on the regular appropriations acts is delayed, however, one or more continuing appropriations acts (also referred to as a continuing resolution, or CR) may be used to provide interim budget authority in order to prevent a funding gap or the need for a shutdown of government activities.

claims.claim: REMOVED, out-of-source proper noun found by round 1: my replacement text opened the regulation section with "The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act says otherwise." That popular name appears in NONE of the registered sources - not in 2 U.S.C. 658c, which cites only its amending public laws, not in 2 U.S.C. 658, and not in any of the four CRS reports. Grep-confirmed both by the verifier and by me. The sentence now names the statute section instead, and 2 U.S.C. 658 has been fetched and registered so the defined term and its cost measure are quoted rather than assumed.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED and wrong as worded (sweep): "CBO scores bills over the current year plus the following ten fiscal years" - which describes an eleven-year window and matches no authority. The statutory horizon in 2 U.S.C. 653(1) is the fiscal year of effect plus the 4 following fiscal years. The longer windows come from elsewhere and are now attributed there: budget resolutions "have often covered a 10-year period" in recent practice, and statutory PAYGO uses a five-year and a 10-year scorecard.

REMOVED, F-FAIL found by this audit, not the sweep, which graded only the CBO/OMB division of labour as unsourced: "The CBO also does not score regulatory effects ... but not the broader economic costs of the regulation on businesses or consumers. The regulatory impact is analyzed separately by the Office of Management and Budget." The first half is contradicted by 2 U.S.C. 658c(b)(1), which requires the Director to estimate the direct cost of Federal private sector mandates - expressly including costs arising in "any necessary implementing regulation" - at or above a $100,000,000 threshold adjusted annually for inflation, with a parallel $50,000,000 duty for intergovernmental mandates. The second half rests on nothing stored and is gone rather than reworded.

REMOVED, U-FLAG: every invented figure on the page. "$50 billion over ten years", "raises taxes by $30 billion", "between $20 billion and $60 billion with a central estimate of $40 billion", "adds $200 billion to the deficit", and - the worst of them - a fabricated quotation of a score: "the CBO estimates annual savings of $2.5 billion, but actual savings could be substantially lower if utilization rates are higher than projected." None of it came from any source; the last was presented as if quoting a real CBO document. All removed, not replaced with substitutes.

REMOVED, F-UNSOURCED (sweep): "A CBO cost estimate for a significant piece of legislation typically runs five to thirty pages." No authority for the range. Replaced with what 2 U.S.C. 653 actually requires an estimate to contain.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "Dynamic scores are less reliable than conventional scores because they require modeling complex economic relationships." That is one side of a live argument stated as fact. CRS R46233 sets out both - proponents on accuracy and comparability, opponents on uncertainty - and records that dynamic estimates have been used for informational purposes rather than for rule compliance. Both sides are now on the page, attributed, and dated to the report.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "This dynamic creates strategic behavior around CBO scores. Legislation is sometimes structured specifically to produce a favorable score ... This practice is sometimes called a budget gimmick." Unsourced characterisation of motive. The sourced replacement is narrower and checkable: the baseline rules themselves determine how a proposal scores, including the asymmetry between expiring tax provisions and expiring programs above the $50 million outlay line.

REMOVED, U-FLAG (sweep): "The CBO doesn't recommend legislation. It doesn't say whether a bill is good or bad policy. It answers one question with professional rigor." Unsourced characterisation, including the flourish "with professional rigor." Replaced with what 2 U.S.C. 601 and 602 actually establish - the appointment test, the four-year term, removal by resolution, and the duty to provide information to named committees.

CHANGED, F-UNSOURCED (sweep): the page described CBO general duties without any statute behind them, and 2 U.S.C. 601 - the only Title 2 section stored when the sweep ran - covers structure and personnel rather than estimating duties. 2 U.S.C. 602 (duties and functions), 653 (analysis) and 658c (mandate statements) were fetched for this audit and now carry those claims.

CHANGED: two of the three Key Sources were cbo.gov pages and the third a congress.gov bill page, none of which the article drew on and none of which a scripted check can fetch. The box and the JSON-LD citation array now list the five U.S. Code sections and four CRS reports the page quotes, with cbo.gov/cost-estimates kept as the place a reader actually goes for a score.

The advisory that dateModified had not moved is expected - publish-article --refresh stamps it.

ROUND 1 hostile Sonnet confirmation pass on frozen text (2026-09-01, fresh agent after the prior session died mid-round; the earlier unreported round does not count under the GENUINE-READ rule): 0 BLOCKING, 6 ADVISORY. The agent read nine of the ten registered sources end-to-end and grep-confirmed every span it did not read in place. It independently re-derived both known prior error classes on this page and found them correctly fixed: the statutory estimating horizon is 2 U.S.C. 653(1)'s "the fiscal year in which it is to become effective and in each of the 4 fiscal years following" (year of effect plus four, NOT ten), and 2 U.S.C. 658c(b)(1) does require the Director to price Federal private-sector mandates at or above 00,000,000 including costs arising "(or in any necessary implementing regulation)", so the removed "CBO does not score regulatory effects" claim is contradicted by statute. It also grep-confirmed that none of the previously removed fabrications — including the invented CBO score quotation — has crept back. ADJUDICATION by the resuming Opus session, each item re-derived from source: (1) ACCEPTED and FIXED — the direct-cost span sits in 2 U.S.C. 658 paragraph (3)(B) ("Direct costs"), not (2) ("Amount", an unrelated grant/loan definition); section repointed. (2) ACCEPTED and FIXED IN PROSE — the 658(7) quotation stopped after "upon the private sector" and substituted a comma for the statute's "except—", which made a truncated definition read as a complete one. The quotation now runs the full paragraph (7) including both exceptions and prong (B), and the framing reads "defined broadly, with two carve-outs"; the ledger span was extended to match. (3) ACCEPTED and FIXED — R46240 carries no "Statutory PAYGO" heading; the scorecard sentence sits under the "Sequestration" heading, which the section pointer now says. (4) ACCEPTED and FIXED IN PROSE — "the two behave differently in a score and differently during a funding lapse" was synthesis: no registered source says direct spending keeps paying out during a lapse, and the government-shutdown article in this same batch REMOVED a flat mandatory-programs claim as an error, so asserting it here would have put two live pages in contradiction. Replaced with a sourced statement that delay on the regular appropriations acts is what opens the funding gap behind a shutdown, receipted to R46240's Continuing Resolutions section, with the sibling link preserved. (5) DISMISSED — "Cost estimates are published on cbo.gov" is wayfinding about a website, not a claim of law or figure; the URL is carried in Key Sources and npm run link-check resolves it (bot-walled, live for humans). (6) ACCEPTED and FIXED IN PROSE — "across the periods it examines" (plural) overstated R46233, whose Summary treats it as one span ("During this period"). The sentence now quotes CRS's own "In most years since 1997, congressional rules have existed..." to supply the antecedent and reads "during that period", and that quote is ledgered. ALSO ADJUDICATED AND DELIBERATELY NOT CHANGED: the two statutory quotations render the source files' — entities as a spaced em-dash ("means — (A)"). That is the published house style (senate-filibuster, already live, is spaced throughout), it is uniform across this article and its batch siblings, and it changes no word of the statute — a rendering choice for an entity-encoded dash, not an altered quotation. Distinguish this from budget-reconciliation, where the source carries a LITERAL unspaced em-dash in running CRS prose and the article was internally inconsistent about it; that one was fixed toward the source.
